lesson.title: Overwhelming a Target with Sheer Numbers
lesson.summary: A distributed denial of service, or DDoS, attack floods a target with traffic from many different sources at once, exhausting its network capacity or processing resources until legitimate users can no longer be served.
lesson.body:
A computer network has finite capacity: a given link can only carry so much traffic per second, and a given server can only process so many requests per second. A denial of service attack aims to consume that finite capacity with illegitimate traffic, so there's nothing left for legitimate users. The distributed part of DDoS refers to how that traffic is generated: rather than one machine sending traffic as fast as it can, which is comparatively easy to identify and block by its single source, an attacker coordinates traffic from many machines simultaneously, often a large number of compromised devices under the attacker's control, sometimes called a botnet. Traffic arriving from thousands of different sources at once is far harder to distinguish from a genuine surge of legitimate demand and far harder to block by simply filtering a handful of addresses.

The effect on the target network is the important part to understand clearly. When the volume of incoming traffic exceeds what a link or a server can actually handle, packets start getting dropped rather than processed, a condition covered earlier as packet loss. Under normal conditions, some packet loss is an occasional, tolerable fact of network life. Under a DDoS attack, the loss becomes severe and sustained, and legitimate requests get dropped right alongside the attack traffic, or never even get a chance to be sent in the first place because the link is already saturated. From the perspective of a real user trying to reach the target, the service is effectively unreachable, which is the entire point of the attack: not to steal anything, but to deny availability.

DDoS attacks come in more than one flavor, and it's worth knowing the general categories rather than treating flooding a target with raw traffic as the whole story. Some attacks simply aim to saturate network bandwidth with volume. Others aim at a server's processing resources rather than its network link, sending traffic that looks individually reasonable but is expensive for the server to handle, gradually exhausting memory, connection slots, or CPU rather than link capacity. The SYN flood, covered as the final chapter in this unit, is a well known example of this second category: it doesn't need to saturate a network link at all, it exhausts a very specific, limited resource on the target server by exploiting exactly how the TCP three way handshake works.
